q: Why do two carbon tools give different Scope 3 totals for the same purchase data?
title: Why two tools give different Scope 3 totals
short: Two tools give different Scope 3 totals from the same purchases because they use different methods and factors: one may multiply rupee spend by an economic factor while the other multiplies tonnes by a material factor. Currency, GST, factor year, region and category mapping each move the result. Compare a sample of lines, not the totals.
audience: Procurement leads comparing vendor outputs; consultants

ul: Method: spend-based (rupees x kg CO2e per unit of currency) against average-data (tonnes x kg CO2e per kg) against supplier-specific. On the same purchase these can differ by a factor of two or more.
Factor database and region: a US or UK input-output factor applied to Indian purchases, against a multi-regional model such as EXIOBASE with an India region, against a material factor.
Currency and price basis: the exchange rate used, the base year of the factor, and whether inflation since that year was removed.
Tax: whether GST was stripped before applying a spend factor. Leaving 18% GST in raises a spend-based figure by 18%.
Category mapping: the same line placed in Category 1 by one tool and Category 2 or 4 by another, or counted in two places.
Boundary and gases: whether factors are cradle-to-gate, include transport, and use AR5 or AR6 global warming potentials.
Duplicates: the same invoice uploaded twice, or a credit note not netted off.

ol: Export both at line level, not as category totals.
Pick the 20 largest lines by emissions in either tool.
For each line compare five things: quantity or spend, unit, factor value, factor unit and source, and category.
Mark which difference explains the gap: method, factor, currency, tax, category or duplicate.
Agree one rule for each cause and apply it to the full dataset.

p: Neither total is right by default. Prefer the line that uses a physical quantity with a factor for that material and country over a spend-based line, and a supplier's own verified figure over both. A spend-based figure is still a fair estimate when it is the only data you have, as long as it is labelled as spend-based with wider uncertainty.

example.title: Worked example: one steel purchase, three results
lines: Purchase: 12 t of steel sections, Rs 10,00,000 before GST
Tool A, spend-based, GST stripped: 10,00,000 / 85 Rs per USD = USD 11,765 x 0.8 kg CO2e per USD (illustrative) = 9,412 kg, about 9.4 t
Tool A, GST left in: 11,80,000 / 85 = USD 13,882 x 0.8 = 11,106 kg, about 11.1 t (18% higher)
Tool B, average-data: 12,000 kg x 2.0 kg CO2e per kg (illustrative) = 24,000 kg, 24 t
Same purchase: 9.4 t, 11.1 t or 24 t depending on method and tax treatment
example.note: The exchange rate and both factors are illustrative, chosen only to show how the gap opens. Real factors depend on the database, year and region.

senseible: Senseible shows the quantity, factor and source behind every line, and labels spend-based estimates as spend-based with wider uncertainty, so its figures can be lined up against another tool's line by line. It does not audit or adjust another vendor's output.
